source: Flow Rate and Continuity
For a liquid filling a pipe, the flow rate Av is the same everywhere: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
Students think water slows down where a pipe gets narrower.

Put your thumb over the end of a garden hose and the water shoots out faster. Nothing new pushed it; the water simply had to get through a smaller opening. This lesson turns that into a rule, using the pressure picture of a liquid and a proportion.

A liquid barely compresses. In a pipe that is full, water cannot pile up anywhere, so every second the same volume must pass every cross-section. In a time $\Delta t$ the water moves a distance $v\,\Delta t$, so the volume passing is $A v\,\Delta t$, and the volume per second is $$Q = Av.$$ If $Q$ is the same at two places, then $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$. Halve the area and the speed must double.
Flow rate $Q = Av$ (in $\text{m}^3\text{/s}$; $1\,\text{L} = 10^{-3}\,\text{m}^3$). For a liquid filling a pipe, $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$: the liquid moves fastest where the pipe is narrowest.
The same volume per second passes both sections, so the water speeds up in the narrow part.
Worked examples
Water moves at $1.5\,\text{m/s}$ in a hose of area $2.0\,\text{cm}^2$. The nozzle opening is $0.50\,\text{cm}^2$. How fast does the water leave?
A nozzle
The areas form a ratio, so they can stay in $\text{cm}^2$.
Water flows at $2.5\,\text{m/s}$ through a pipe of area $4.0\,\text{cm}^2$. What is the flow rate, and how long does a $10\,\text{L}$ bucket take to fill?
Filling a bucket
Convert the area: $4.0\,\text{cm}^2 = 4.0 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{m}^2$.
A round pipe narrows from a diameter of $4.0\,\text{cm}$ to $2.0\,\text{cm}$. Water moves at $0.50\,\text{m/s}$ in the wide part. How fast in the narrow part?
Half the diameter
Area goes as diameter squared ($A = \pi d^2/4$), so $\dfrac{A_1}{A_2} = \left(\dfrac{4.0}{2.0}\right)^2 = 4$.
$v_2 = (0.50\,\text{m/s})(4) = 2.0\,\text{m/s}$. Half the diameter means four times the speed.

Thinking water slows down where a pipe narrows, as if it were squeezed or held back. In a full pipe it must speed up, or the water behind it would have nowhere to go. Rivers show it too: the same water that drifts through a wide, deep pool races through narrow rapids. Check: does $A \times v$ come out the same at both places?
Air compresses, so $A_1 v_1 = A_2 v_2$ holds for a gas only when its density stays about the same, as in slow airflow.
